intro: Marketing managers combine analysis, persuasion and judgment, the core of most executive roles. The closest of the 25 careers below is Purchasing Managers, with an 85% skill match and a BLS May 2025 median of $148,080, which is 11% less than the $166,790 marketing managers earn.
why_it_works: Running marketing means reading data, choosing where to spend and persuading leaders and customers at the same time. O*NET rates complex problem solving, judgment, persuasion and systems evaluation at 3.88 out of 5 for this job. Finance, HR and executive roles use the same strategic skills. Because pay is already high, only 4 matches pay more. The gaps are leading people and teaching others.
tips: Chief Executives earn $213,990, which is 28% more, and marketing is a common route to the top job.
Financial Managers earn almost the same as you, $166,570, and value your budget and analytics skills.
Build a team or mentor juniors; managing people is your most common skill gap.

faq.q: What jobs can former marketing managers do?
faq.a: The closest matches are Purchasing Managers (85%), Financial Managers (80%) and Compensation and Benefits Managers (79%), based on O*NET 31.0. Human Resources Managers are 78% matched and earn $149,280, which is 10% less than the $166,790 marketing manager median.

faq.q: Which careers for marketing managers pay more?
faq.a: Only 4 of the 25 matches pay more. Chief Executives earn $213,990 (28% more), Industrial-Organizational Psychologists $193,950 (16% more) and Computer and Information Systems Managers $175,140 (5% more), according to BLS May 2025 data. The first two usually need a graduate degree.

faq.q: Do marketing managers need another degree?
faq.a: Usually not. 20 of the 25 matches need no more education than marketing managers already have, while 5 usually need a graduate degree. A bachelor's degree is common, held by 53% of workers in the closest match, so your results count most.

faq.q: What skills should marketing managers build?
faq.a: The skills that most often need work are managing people, service orientation, managing financial resources and instructing. Systems evaluation already rates 3.88 out of 5 for marketing managers in O*NET, so leading and developing teams is the main step toward executive roles.
